title: Tic-tac-toe class model
idea: A tic-tac-toe model is a handful of small types (game, board, player, move, symbol) where one owner, the `Game`, checks every rule before any state changes.
points: Nouns in the requirements become types: `Game`, `Player`, `Move`, `Symbol`, the board.
Values with no identity are records or enums: a `Move` is just two coordinates.
`Game` owns the cells privately, so every rule lives in one method.
A rejected move throws and keeps the turn; only legal moves change state.

hero.title: The classes and who owns what

steps.caption: Read the requirements for nouns: game, board, player, move, mark. Each becomes a type.
The caller builds a `Move` value and hands it over. It never touches the cells.
`Game` owns the cells. Range, free cell and turn checks all happen inside `play`.
`Game` holds two players in turn order. The constructor rejects two players with one symbol.
`Symbol` is an enum, so a cell can only hold X, O or nothing. No stray characters.

code.title: The problem: no owner
code.caption: An unguarded array and an unchecked `play`: moves steal cells, strangers write, bad input crashes.

walk.text: The board and turn are package-visible fields. Nothing guards them.
`play` writes first and never asks whether the cell is free or on the board.
X overwrites O's centre cell. The game accepts it silently.
Any code can write a third symbol, because a `char` allows any character.
An off-board move surfaces as an array crash, not a clear rule message.
The illegal steal still counted as X's turn. Legal and illegal moves look the same.

code.title: The fix: types and rules
code.caption: Small value types plus one `Game` that checks every rule before it changes anything.

walk.text: Values are an enum and records: immutable, with `equals` and readable `toString` for free.
All state is private and final where possible. Only `Game` can change the cells.
The constructor enforces setup rules: a real board size and two different symbols.
Every move is checked first. A clear message names the broken rule.
State changes only after all checks pass, so a rejected move keeps the turn.
Callers get a text copy of the board, never the array itself.
The caller sees each rejection. The next legal move still belongs to the right player.

pitfalls: Returning the `Symbol[][]` array lets callers write cells; return a copy or text.
Checking 'cell taken' only in the UI breaks once a bot or API sends moves.
Switching turns before validating hands the opponent a free move after a rejection.

quiz.q: An interviewer asks where the rule 'a cell can be played only once' belongs. Best answer?
options: In the UI, before it calls `play`
In `Game.play`, which owns the board state
In `Player`, since players make the moves
quiz.why: The rule depends on board state. Only the class that owns the cells can check it, and every caller passes through `play`.

takeaway: One owner checks every rule; everything else is a small value type.

starters: Should Board be its own class or stay inside Game?
Why use an enum for Symbol instead of a char?
